paras: The lynching of Jose Francisco Gallegos and Thomas Valdez took place one night in October 1880 at Conejos, Colorado, when armed men took the two prisoners from the jail and hanged them from a nearby tree. The two men, described in the press as Mexicans, were awaiting trial for the murder of a traveler named S. Duprez, which they had reportedly confessed at a preliminary hearing in Albuquerque. Two New Mexico papers reported the lynching with approval, one under the headline "Retributive Justice."

In August 1880 a Denver dispatch reported that two Mexicans, "Gallegh and Valdez," had been arrested at Albuquerque on suspicion of murder and had made a full confession at a preliminary hearing there. The dead man was named as S. Duprez, said to have been a sheep owner in southern Colorado, and the prisoners were said to have taken $1,200, a check, post-office orders, two horses and a wagon, with $406 found on them. According to the dispatch, Duprez had stopped overnight in a tent while traveling south, and one man shot him as he slept while the other stood by with an axe.

The Golden Gate, as reprinted in Las Vegas, gave the hearing as held before Justice Duran and placed the killing somewhere near Conejos, with the arrest made as the men traveled toward Nacimiento. The same paper reported that the prisoners had tried to break jail and were kept chained to the door with log chains. After a summer in the Albuquerque jail, the two were taken to Conejos County for trial, according to the New Mexican by a sheriff whose name the print renders as "Carril!".

A few days after the prisoners arrived at Conejos, a "body of armed men" entered the jail at night, took both men out and hanged them from the limbs of a neighboring tree. The New Mexican, relying on a man who came directly from Conejos, said the lynching was done "quietly" and that the town's residents learned of it from the bodies the next morning. The Albuquerque Journal described the men only as "reported" to have been taken from jail and lynched.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the lynching party, or other official response appears in the coverage.

The case first reached newspapers across the country in August, when the Denver dispatch on the confession ran in papers from Washington and New York to Salt Lake City and Butte, and in German in Missouri. Even then the Golden Gate called the prisoners "fiends in human shape" and wrote that they "ought to be spirited away" never to be heard of again.

The lynching itself drew far less attention: only two accounts, both from New Mexico papers, were found, each surviving as a reprint. The Las Vegas Morning Gazette reprinted the New Mexican's report on October 26 under the heading "Retributive Justice," describing a lynching done "quietly and clean ly." The Cheyenne Transporter in Indian Territory carried the Albuquerque Journal's version on November 10, which reminded readers of the "fiendish crime" and said they would not be sorry justice had been done to the men "although by a mob."

Reports differ on who the dead man was: the August dispatch called Duprez a sheep owner, the New Mexican a prospector, and the Albuquerque Journal a Frenchman, while one telegraphic item gave his initial as "L." The Golden Gate said the men found Duprez asleep in his own tent, whereas a Butte paper's summary had him stopping overnight in the prisoners' tent; the Golden Gate's version came from the hearing itself.

A 'body of armed men' took both men out of jail and hanged them from a tree, and both reprinted accounts present the killing as justice for the murder the men were accused of (A21, A23).

Two separate New Mexico papers, the New Mexican (reprinted in A21) and the Albuquerque Journal (reprinted in A23), independently report that the pair were taken from jail and lynched, though both rest on second-hand word from Conejos.
